stem: Two independent events A and B have probabilities P(A) = 2/3 and P(B) = 3/4. What is the probability that at least one of the two events occurs?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Computing P(A and B) = P(A)*P(B) = (2/3)*(3/4) = 1/2, solving for the joint event instead of the at-least-one event.
Computing P(neither) = (1/3)*(1/4) = 1/12 and then mistakenly subtracting from 1/2 rather than from 1, giving 5/12.
Adding the complement probabilities P(A') + P(B') = 1/3 + 1/4 = 7/12 instead of multiplying them to get P(neither), then treating that sum as P(neither) and subtracting from 1.

explanation: For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A)*P(B). The complement approach for at-least-one is fastest: P(at least one) = 1 - P(none) = 1 - P(A')*P(B') = 1 - (1/3)*(1/4) = 11/12.

explanation_sections.punchline: At-least-one is most cleanly solved via its complement: 1 minus the probability that neither occurs.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify the model: at-least-one for independent events using complement. P(A') = 1/3, P(B') = 1/4. Since independent, P(neither) = (1/3)(1/4) = 1/12. P(at least one) = 1 - 1/12 = 11/12.
explanation_sections.lesson: For independent events, use the complement formula P(at least one) = 1 - product of all complements.
explanation_sections.timing: 70 seconds. Compute both complements, multiply, subtract from 1. The trap is computing P(A and B) = 1/2 instead.
